cues.text: Start with the surface view board.
A points into the stomatal pore, the space between the two guard cells.
B points to the left guard cell.
C identifies a selected chloroplast, while D points to the larger nucleus.
A pore is not a third cell, and a chloroplast is not the nucleus.
The surrounding outline locates an epidermal region without specifying a fixed
subsidiary cell pattern.
Selected organelles are shown rather than their complete number or
distribution.
Trace each leader line to its endpoint before naming the structure.
This is a view of the leaf surface, not the transverse section used in the
previous class.
Examine the heavier curves facing the pore.
They represent the thicker inner walls of these kidney shaped guard cells.
The outer walls, away from the pore, are represented more lightly.
Different wall properties and cellulose arrangement help convert changes in
turgor into changes in cell shape.
Guard cells normally contain chloroplasts, unlike most ordinary leaf epidermal
cells.
This does not make every epidermal cell a guard cell, nor does it mean
photosynthesis alone completely explains stomatal movement.
The drawing represents wall differences schematically, not a numerical
thickness measurement.
Use the pore facing direction to identify an inner wall rather than whichever
line happens to be nearest the page centre.
Move to the grass type board.
G identifies a guard cell with expanded ends and a narrow middle portion,
giving the familiar dumbbell outline.
P indicates the pore between the pair.
S marks selected flanking subsidiary cells.
Subsidiary cells are specialised neighbours, not extra guard cells enclosing a
second pore.
Their arrangement varies among stomatal types, so the two cells drawn here are
not a universal rule.
In standard comparisons, grasses commonly have dumbbell shaped guard cells,
whereas kidney shaped guard cells occur widely in other plants.
Do not turn the grass example into a claim that every monocot species must
share exactly this shape.
Use the two surface boards together.
In the standard anatomical description, the stomatal apparatus includes the
pore, the guard cells and associated subsidiary cells when present.
Ordinary surrounding epidermal cells should not automatically be assigned
specialised subsidiary status without evidence.
Both boards show a pore guarded by a pair of cells even though the cell
outlines differ.
A selected surface drawing does not establish the whole leaf's venation,
whether all stomata occur on one surface, or the plant's species.
First identify the view and the local label endpoints, then state what the
visible structures support.
Avoid carrying letter meanings from one figure into another.
The state comparison uses kidney shaped guard cells.
A represents higher guard cell turgor and a wider pore.
B represents lower turgor and a closed pore, with the inner boundaries
meeting.
The guard cells do not disappear when the pore closes.
Changes in guard cell solute content influence water potential, and water
movement by osmosis alters turgor.
The cell walls constrain expansion, so increased turgor changes shape rather
than simply enlarging every dimension equally.
This is a conceptual comparison, not a measured time series or a claim that
every species has the same response speed.
Keep the water movement, turgor change and aperture change in a connected
explanation.
Add control carefully.
Potassium ions and other solutes participate in guard cell osmotic changes; a
cartoon should not be read as proof that potassium is the only relevant
substance.
Abscisic acid signalling can promote stomatal closure during water stress.
Many plants open stomata in daylight and close them at night, but that pattern
is not universal.
CAM plants commonly take up carbon dioxide through open stomata at night.
Environmental conditions, internal carbon dioxide and water status also
influence the aperture.
The two states shown here do not supply a clock, hormone measurement or ion
channel experiment.
They illustrate the endpoint of a regulated process.
The final board changes to a schematic leaf section.
A points to the opening between the selected guard cell sections.
B identifies the substomatal air space immediately below, and C points to
surrounding mesophyll.
The air space communicates with intercellular spaces inside the leaf.
It is not a water filled vessel or a missing organelle.
Compare this view with the surface sketches: a pair of oval sections cannot by
itself establish the complete three dimensional outline of the guard cells.
View orientation matters.
Identify the outside, the epidermal opening and the internal air space pathway
before interpreting the gas arrows.
Read the arrows as one illustrative situation: an illuminated leaf with net
photosynthetic carbon dioxide uptake.
Carbon dioxide is shown entering, while water vapour is shown leaving.
Diffusion follows gradients, so the arrows are not permanent one way valves or
a rule for every time of day.
Water loss through the pore occurs as vapour, not as a stream of liquid water
in a xylem vessel.
A wider aperture can influence exchange, but actual rates also depend on
humidity, temperature, air movement and other conditions.
The board gives no numerical flux or complete oxygen balance.
Explain the represented situation and its limits rather than treating every
arrow as universal.
